q: What is an LLM, in one minute?
a: A decoder-only Transformer trained on huge text corpora to predict the next token. Text is tokenized, embedded, processed by stacked attention + feed-forward blocks, and the last position's output is turned into a probability distribution over the vocabulary. Generation repeats this token by token. Instruction tuning and preference tuning make it a helpful assistant.

q: Is a token the same as a word?
a: No. Tokens are sub-word units: whole words, word pieces, punctuation or whitespace. English averages about 0.75 words per token, but code, numbers and many Indian languages need more tokens per word. Always measure with the model's tokenizer.

Start from characters (or bytes). Repeatedly find the most frequent adjacent pair in the corpus and merge it into a new token, until the vocabulary reaches the target size. At inference, apply the learned merges in order. Frequent words become single tokens; rare words split into pieces, so nothing is out-of-vocabulary.

q: Why are LLMs bad at counting letters in a word?
a: They see tokens, not characters. "strawberry" may be one or two tokens, so the model has no direct view of individual letters and must rely on memorised spelling patterns.

q: Why does tokenization matter for cost and RAG?
a: API pricing, context limits and rate limits are counted in tokens. RAG chunk sizes must be measured in the embedding model's tokens to stay under its input limit, and the final prompt must fit the LLM's context window with room for the answer.

q: Encoder-only vs decoder-only vs encoder–decoder: which for what?
a: Encoder-only (BERT): bidirectional, best for classification, NER, embeddings and reranking. Decoder-only (GPT, LLaMA, Claude): causal, best for generation, chat, agents. Encoder–decoder (T5, BART): input-to-output tasks like translation and summarisation.

They are trained to produce plausible next tokens, not to verify facts. When knowledge is missing, rare or ambiguous, the most plausible continuation can be wrong but fluent. Training also rewards always answering. RAG, citations, abstention instructions and verification reduce it.

q: What is the context window, and does a bigger one remove the need for RAG?
a: The maximum number of tokens (prompt + output) the model can process at once. Bigger windows help but don't replace RAG: cost and latency grow with prompt length, models miss facts buried in the middle of long prompts, you lose citations and per-user access control, and most corpora are far bigger than any window.

q: Why does the same text cost more tokens in Hindi or in code than in English?
a: Tokenizers are trained mostly on English text, so common English words are single tokens while other scripts, rare words, numbers and code get split into many small pieces. More tokens means higher cost, less room in the context window and sometimes worse quality.
